name: Habushu
description: Okinawan awamori with a habu pit viper coiled in the bottle, usually sweetened with honey and steeped with herbs. The snake is the point: it is left in the flask for months, and the spirit takes on a faintly savoury, medicinal weight the base rice spirit does not have on its own.
funFact: Producers chill the snake until it is torpid, then lower it into the flask — where the alcohol fixes it mid-strike. The open jaws in a display bottle are set by the ethanol, not by taxidermy.

serve.how: Poured neat at room temperature in very small measures, usually as a tonic at the end of a meal rather than a drink you sit with. Honey-sweetened bottlings are the gentler introduction.

composition.summary: Long-grain rice awamori infused with a whole habu viper, honey and herbs.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Awamori distilled from Thai indica rice with black koji

components.label: Infusion
components.detail: One whole habu pit viper, steeped for months

components.label: Sweetening
components.detail: Honey and up to a dozen herbs in most commercial bottlings

composition.process: The viper is steeped whole rather than for flavour extraction alone — the practice is tonic and totemic as much as culinary, and Okinawan makers sell it on longevity rather than taste.

name: Sodabi
description: Benin's palm-wine distillate, made by fermenting the sap of the oil palm and running it through simple pot stills. It is the spirit poured on the ground in Vodun ceremony before anyone drinks, which makes it ritual equipment as much as a drink.
funFact: It carries the name of Bonaventure Kpodji Sodabi, a Beninese soldier who learned distilling in France during the First World War and brought the method home around 1919.

serve.how: Neat and at room temperature, in small measures, and traditionally with a first splash poured to the ground for the ancestors before the glass reaches a mouth.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sap tapped from the oil palm, fermented into palm wine

components.label: Fermentation
components.detail: Wild yeasts, one to three days in the heat

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Small pot stills, frequently improvised

composition.process: Sap ferments within hours of tapping, so distillation happens close to the tree. Strength varies widely between producers because almost none of it is standardised.

name: Klekovača
description: Plum rakija redistilled over juniper berries, the Balkan answer to the question of what happens when a fruit brandy meets a gin botanical. The juniper does not mask the plum so much as sit alongside it, resinous and cold.
funFact: The name comes from kleka, the local word for juniper — and it is shared with a mountain in western Bosnia, which is why bottles and maps sometimes confuse people.

serve.how: Room temperature or barely cool, never iced, in a small tulip glass before a meal. Chilling it hard flattens the juniper, which is the entire reason the drink exists.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Plum rakija, usually from Požegača plums

components.label: Botanical
components.detail: Wild juniper berries, macerated then redistilled

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Often rested in glass demijohns rather than wood

composition.process: Redistilling rather than simply macerating keeps it clear and stops the juniper turning bitter, which is what separates it from the many home infusions that share the name.

name: Chinguirito
description: Mexico's contraband cane spirit, distilled from raw sugarcane juice or piloncillo on the Veracruz coast. For most of its history it was defined less by how it was made than by the fact that making it was a crime.
funFact: The Spanish Crown banned it in 1631 to protect brandy shipped from Spain, and the ban held for 165 years. When the Crown finally legalised it in 1796 it promptly taxed it to pay for coastal fortifications.

serve.how: Neat in a small tumbler, or lengthened with lime and soda in the coastal style. The modern artisanal bottlings reward drinking it the way you would a rhum agricole blanc.

composition.summary: Fresh sugarcane juice or piloncillo, fermented and pot distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Pressed cane juice, or piloncillo dissolved in water

components.label: Fermentation
components.detail: Open vats with wild yeast

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper or clay pot stills

composition.process: Because it was illegal for so long the method was never standardised, and the surviving recipes are regional rather than national. Small Veracruz producers have revived it since the 2010s.

name: Chuchuhuasi
description: Amazonian bark macerated in cane aguardiente, usually cut with honey. It is sold by the jar in the markets of Iquitos and Pucallpa, closer to a household remedy than a bar bottle, and it tastes like one.
funFact: The bark comes from Maytenus laevis, a rainforest tree whose name in Quechua means roughly trembling back — a reference to the rheumatism it was long steeped to treat.

serve.how: A small measure at room temperature after eating, taken as a digestif. Market versions are steeped for weeks and vary enormously between sellers.

composition.summary: Maytenus laevis bark steeped in cane aguardiente with honey.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Cane aguardiente from the Peruvian Amazon

components.label: Botanical
components.detail: Chuchuhuasi bark, steeped for weeks to months

components.label: Sweetening
components.detail: Wild honey, sometimes with cinnamon or clove

composition.process: Maceration rather than distillation, so nothing is stripped out — the tannin from the bark is what gives it the dry, drying grip on the finish.

name: Yaa Dong
description: Thailand's roadside macerations — roots, bark and herbs steeped in lao khao rice spirit and sold by the shot from big glass jars. There is no single recipe; every stall keeps its own, and the jar you are pointed at depends on what you say is wrong with you.
funFact: The name means roughly preserved medicine, and it is sold as one — stalls organise their jars by complaint rather than by flavour, which is why a chaser is usually handed over with the glass.

serve.how: One small shot at room temperature, taken quickly, with a chaser of soda or a slice of fruit. It is a street-stall drink rather than a sipping spirit, and it is not built to be lingered over.

composition.summary: Roots, bark and herbs macerated in lao khao rice spirit.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Lao khao, unaged Thai rice spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Dozens of roots, barks and dried herbs, varying by stall

components.label: Sweetening
components.detail: Palm sugar or honey in many recipes

composition.process: Maceration for weeks in glass jars, topped up rather than emptied, so a long-running jar is never quite the same drink twice.

name: Pox
description: The Maya ceremonial spirit of the Chiapas highlands, distilled from maize, sugarcane and wheat bran. It is still poured in Tzotzil ritual, and the bottles that reach bars outside Mexico are a recent and slightly awkward second life for it.
funFact: Pox means medicine in Tzotzil, and it is pronounced posh. It is still used in ceremonies at the church of San Juan Chamula, where it sits alongside candles and copal rather than behind a bar.

serve.how: Neat at room temperature in a small cup. It is softer and sweeter than mezcal and does not need the ceremony of salt or citrus that agave spirits attract.

composition.summary: Maize, sugarcane and wheat bran, fermented together and pot distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Cracked maize with piloncillo or cane juice

components.label: Adjunct
components.detail: Wheat bran, which drives the bread-dough note

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper or clay pot stills in highland Chiapas

composition.process: The maize is the ritual ingredient and the cane is the fermentable — which is why it reads sweet rather than starchy, and why it sits closer to a light rum than to a corn whiskey.
